articles.title: Act for Nutrition conference: Experts call for multisectoral approach, community-led intervention in addressing malnutrition crisis
articles.description: Day 1 of the two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’ — held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel — concluded on Wednesday, with experts urging urgent action on Pakistan’s malnutrition and stunting crisis, with a focus on multisectoral interventions. With more than 40 per cent of children under five stunted, a maternal mortality rate of 155 deaths per 100,000 live births, and malnutrition costing Pakistan upwards of $17 billion annually, the country stands at a crossroads: continue on the current trajectory and surrender an entire generation’s potential, or choose a different future. The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action. The focus of discussions will be on moving the national conversation beyond statistics towards practical, measurable interventions that can improve nutrition outcomes and protect Pakis­tan’s human capital and future generations. View the full agenda here . 5:27pm - Day 1 of the conference concludes 5:15pm - Researcher calls for nutrition-related interventions at community, systemic levels Director at the International Research Force Dr Hana Mahmood said focus on nutrition was needed at the community, systemic, and legislative levels. Remarking on awareness campaigns on the community level, she said, “Interventions are not designed according to the latest theories and latest approaches towards designing behaviour change”. She stressed a multisectoral approach to nutrition, adding that “no specific industry owns nutrition”. 5:00pm - Doctor stresses rigorous testing for pregnant women Dr Nosheen Ashraf of the National Institutes of Health, speaking about maternal nutrition, said that during antenatal visits, mothers are asked to take supplements to address nutritional deficiencies; however, she noted a lack of consistent monitoring. Dr Ashraf said there were not enough laboratories in far-flung areas, as she called for rigorous testing of pregnant mothers to track any nutritional deficiencies. 4:55pm - Gynaecologist stresses nutrition should not be limited to pregnancy or childbirth Capital Hospital Associate Gynaecologist Dr Urooj Yasir Khan said the focus of nutrition should not be limited to pregnancy or childbirth. “There is hardly any awareness about nutrition in our adolescent girl groups.” Following a substantial loss of iron during menstruation, micronutrient deficiencies in the body at the onset of pregnancy, especially if it’s a teenage pregnancy, can lead to growth-restricted babies, she said. Commenting on treatment for obesity, she said, “we don’t say what’s important to eat”, adding that the focus seems to be on the number of calories consumed. 4:53pm - Founder Nutradevice calls for equitable access to nutritious food Founder Nutradevice Dr Nosheen Taqvi held that creating awareness about nutritious food did not guarantee nutrition; rather, she maintained that it was worth examining “if the mother can access it, implement it, afford it and keeping in view the power of the woman in the household, can she give it to the children”. Dr Taqvi also clarified misconceptions around nutrition. “It is not true that healthy food is always expensive [..] as you don’t always have to focus on animal-based food”. She also noted that mothers in Pakistani households did not prioritise themselves. “Food is given to the family first. and then the mother eats whatever is left of it.” She also noted that stigma around weight gain was leading to nutritional deficiencies in women as well. Founder Nutradevice Dr Nosheen Taqvi speaks at the conference. — White Star 4:38pm - Researcher explains why ‘1,000-day’ period is critical to addressing malnutrition Director of the International Research Force Dr Hana Mahmood explained why the first 1,000-day period of an infant’s life remained critical in addressing malnutrition. “The most important thing we have to attend to right now is that these 1,000 days are those days in which growth is exponentially high and the requirement for micronutrients is massive,” Dr Mahmood said. She added that during this time, the immune system and major organs were developing in such a way that any lack in nutritional input could lead to irreversible damage. “During the first two years of life, 80pc of a child’s brain develops,” she said. Dr Mahmood also noted that Pakistan had one of the highest child-under-five mortality rates, a majority of which was contributed by malnutrition. “250m deaths can be averted by focusing on prevention of stunting,” she said. Director of the International Research Force Dr Hana Mahmood at the conference. — White Star 4:27pm - Session titled ‘First 1,000 days: Why women and girls matter for nutrition’ begins Panelists at the session titled ‘The first 1,000 days: Why women and girls matter for nutrition’. — White Star 4:10pm - Agri consultant highlights need for demand pull in producing nutritionally rich food Agriculture consultant Hasan Khurrum Hanif, talking about producing nutritionally dense food, said, “Pakistani farmers need a demand pull, rather than a supply push”. “Farmers will produce what you pay us to produce and if there is a market where I can sell zinc-fortified wheat, where I can sell vegetables with lower pesticide residue, all of those require a different input package, which has a cost component,” he said. Hanif added that processors needed to provide farmers an ecosystem. 3:55pm - Food safety infrastructure critical for nutrition, economy, says Tetra Pak executive Corporate Affairs Director at Tetra Pak Noor Aftab stressed the significance of food safety, saying that “food systems need to be treated as critical infrastructure”. He said that Pakistan is one of the largest milk-producing countries, but there were no safe milk or pasteurisation laws in the country, depriving the economy of $30bn export potential. He added that in Pakistan, milk is taxed at one of the highest rates in the world. “If there is a resilient food systems infrastructure built within Pakistan, coupled with sustainable fiscal roadmaps... that will allow [...] the infrastructure to act as a catalyst for nourishment and improvement.” Corporate Affairs Director at Tetra Pak Noor Aftab speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Muhammad Asim 3:45pm - Nutrition investment reduced absenteeism rate in Bangladesh, says official Project Manager at the Workforce Nutrition GM Reza Sumon, joining the conference through video conference from Bangladesh, discussed nutrition investments for the workforce. He said that in Bangladesh’s government sector, the anaemia rate within the workforce was at 51.9pc. However, after interventions via funding for fortified rice, oils and iron and folic acid tablets, the anaemia rate dropped to 32pc, Sumon said, which helped convince the private sector to make similar investments in nutrition. He said after the private sector invested $10m in nutrition in the past year, absenteeism in workplaces has reduced from 70pc to 40pc. 3:40pm - EBM executive shares details on a fortified biscuits initiative Head of Corporate Communications & Sustainability at English Biscuit Manufacturers (EBM) Attiyah Inaam Khan shared details of an initiative launched by the company in which fortified biscuits were provided to mothers to address malnutrition. “We tracked them for five years, and mothers who received biscuits showed great iron levels during pregnancy, and children born under the study showed stronger cognitive development,” she recalled. “It is not about margins but more about whether there is evidence on the ground and whether the intervention can be scalable,” she added. “Government can also play a very important lever here: tax credit for fortification in products and reduce the import duty on fortification,” she added. Head of Corporate Communications & Sustainability at English Biscuit Manufacturers (EBM) Attiyah Inaam Khan speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Muhammad Asim 3:36pm - Session on mobilising private capital and partnerships begins A panel discussion on mobilising private capital and partnerships has begun. 3:12pm - ADB views malnutrition as an economic issue, working with BISP, says official Senior Project Officer at Asian Development Bank (ADB) Mansoor Ali Masood said the bank was looking at malnutrition through an economic lens rather than viewing it solely as a health issue. “Hence, we are trying to mainstream it through social protection, education, agriculture and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services,” he said, adding that ADB was supporting the Benazir Nashonuma Programme and had allocated around half of a $960m fund to address stunting. “ADB is supporting the expansion of BNP, helping BISP in expanding the awareness of mothers who are better informed and can take better decisions for their children and ensure dietary diversity.” Senior Project Officer at Asian Development Bank (ADB) Mansoor Ali Masood speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad 3:07pm - ‘Nutrition is part of human capital’ The Dean of Research at Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE) Dr Shujaat Farooq, said that the economic cost of malnutrition was “too much”. Citing statistics, he said 40pc of children in the country are facing stunting while 25 million children are out of school. He added that 75pc of children in schools were unable to learn proficiently due to malnutrition. “Nutrition is part of human capital,” Farooq said. 3:00pm - No multi-sectoral nutrition programmes in the past decade: Planning ministry official Chief of nutrition at the planning ministry, Dr Nazeer Ahmed, said in the past “one to two decades, there had been no major nutrition programme implemented in the provinces, except the Benazir Nashonuma Programme”. “We have the policies in the four provinces, and nutrition strategies [..] But on the ground, we do not have any multi-sectoral programmes implemented,” he said. Panelists at the Building Human Capital and Driving Economic Growth. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 2:55pm - Nutrition not often framed as GDP statistic: Gates Foundation official Gates Foundation Senior Programme Officer of Development Policy and Finance Dr Ammar Malik said that according to World Bank statistics, for every dollar a government invested in nutrition, it could get up to $23 back in the form of economic benefits. Questioning why such a high return on investment was still ignored, Malik said one of the issues was that nutrition investments were long-term, with returns becoming obvious years or decades later. He added another issue was that nutrition is seen as a standalone topic in such discussions, instead of framing it as a gross domestic product statistic. “If I were to say to you that Pakistan is losing 3pc of its GDP because of lack of investment in nutrition, that is a much stronger argument for economic policymakers than it is to talk about nutrition,” he said. 2:50pm - Gates Foundation official says Pakistan’s crisis is a ‘balance sheet problem’ Gates Foundation’s Dr Ammar Malik, who serves as the senior programme officer of development policy and finance, said the nutrition problem in Pakistan was a “balance sheet problem”. “The government of Pakistan can either now decide to spend more on nutrition today through our budgets, or we can pay the price of this lack of investment in the form of lost gross domestic product over the next several years or even decades,” he said. 2:45pm — ‘Nutrition has few dedicated champions’ Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad noted that another reason nutrition was underfunded was a lack of dedicated efforts towards the issue. “Why is this? Well, because malnutrition is multi-sectoral. It is the interaction of poor diet, poor water, poor sanitation, poor healthcare, and poor care in general, and so each of these areas has its own ministry.” “There is no ministry of nutrition,” he added. Panelists at the session titled ‘Building Human Capital and Driving Economic Growth’ at the conference. — White Star 2:42pm — Expert says malnutrition underfunded despite ‘catastrophic consequences’ The session on investing in nutrition began with a video note by Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition Executive Director Lawrence Haddad, who pointed out that malnutrition remained underfunded “despite its catastrophic impact”. “Forty five per cent of children’s deaths under three worldwide are due to malnutrition,” Haddad noted, adding that less than 1pc of international aid was spent on malnutrition. “It is quite invisible in many ways,” he added. 2:30pm — Conference resumes after lunch break 1:50pm - Lunch break The conference will resume at 2:30pm. 1:40pm- WHO official says ‘no bigger risk than lack of action’ Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan warned that “there was no bigger risk than the lack of action” in addressing malnutrition. “As we speak, before I finish answering, [..] in the next three minutes, at least 14 children will have died across the world from causes related to maternal and child malnutrition,” Thom said, adding that such deaths were preventable and “we cannot afford not to take action”. She also noted that Pakistan was suffering an annual economic loss of $17bn due to stunting and malnutrition. Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation speaks at the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 1:34pm - WFP official says malnutrition not just driven by poverty Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that malnutrition was not just driven by poverty. “It is also directly influenced and fed by poor access to services ... health services and water and sanitation services,” he said. 1:15pm - Expert calls for focusing on adolescent nutrition Food security adviser on nutrition and social protection at GIZ Pakistan, Dr Faiza Wahab, raised the alarm at the “missing adolescent middle” during conversations about malnutrition. She said that nutrition discourse had been focused on the first 1,000 days of a child, but she stressed, “we are really missing the middle, which is between childhood and motherhood”. “Focusing on adolescent nutrition is not to prepare them for motherhood, but it is also a window where the investment really returns in the form of human capital development,” she said. She explained that during adolescent years, young girls were vulnerable to anaemia and iron deficiencies due to “rapid growth, hormonal changes and menstruation”. “If she is not empowered, she cannot participate in education, and she has less cognitive capabilities,” Dr Wahab said. Food security adviser on nutrition and social protection at GIZ Pakistan, Dr Faiza Wahab speaks at the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 1:10pm - WHO official stresses need for integrating social protection programmes with health services Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan, said integrating social protection with existing health and nutrition services is important. She said that evidence showed that doing so and strengthening integrated primary healthcare was an effective way of reaching vulnerable families and delivering high-impact nutrition interventions. 1:02pm - WFP official says nutrition is not just about food Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that nutrition was not only about food. “It’s not only about access to food. It is about a healthy diet, the capacity to ensure multi-sectoral intervention and collaboration among us,” he said. He said that it was also necessary to ensure access to a more healthy diet and the design of the social protection was nutrition-sensitive,” he said. Thomas Conan. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 12:50pm - BISP official talks about Nashonuma programme BISP Director General Dr Asim Ijaz spoke about the Benazir Nashonuma Programme (BNP), which he said had added a “nutritional and health layer” to the existing BISP registry. He stressed that there exists a 1,000-day window for a child’s development, during which “irreversible damage can occur”. “This is why BISP changed its thinking in 2019,” he said. He said that the recognition was then realised in the Nashonuma pilot launch in 2020, which was then phased out country-wide in 2021. “Nashonuma itself is not a separate bureaucracy but layered onto existing platforms,” he said, explaining that BISP’s registry was now carrying a nutritional and health layer. “So the idea was to have one beneficiary record with multiple beneficial layers,” he said. 12:42pm - ‘We can no longer afford to look away,’ BISP chairperson says Senator Rubina Khalid, the chairperson of Benazir Income Support Programme, said in her keynote address that the responsibility lay not just with providing financial assistance, but with also helping families move from vulnerability towards dignity. “We have gathered here today ... because we can no longer afford to look away,” she said. She said that more than 40pc of children under five in Pakistan were stunted, while malnutrition placed a huge burden on the economy. “Stunting is not only a health issue. It is a human capital issue, an economic issue and a challenge to Pakistan’s future,” she said. She said that the country lacked integration of the programmes it had to address these issues. At the end of her address, she said: “We must work together so that every child in Pakistan has the opportunity to grow, learn and reach their full potential. Because every child we protect from malnutrition is not simply a life protected, it is the future protected, a family strengthened and a stronger Pakistan secured.” Benazir Income Support Programme Chairperson Senator Rubina Khalid delivers the keynote address. — DawnNewsTV 12:40pm: Session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins A session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins. 12:30pm - Sri Lankan doctor calls for understanding child growth trajectory in South Asia Dr Rannan-Eliya, in answer to a question, pointed out that the child growth trajectory in South Asia was not the same as the rest of the world. “We have sort of misunderstood the problem,” he remarked, adding: “There is no uniformity in child growth, and because we use a single growth standard, we partly misdiagnose what is going on”. “In my sense, Sri Lankan kids need to be better nourished but there is a limit to what we can do and we need to understand that,” he said. He noted that a similar understanding was also being realised in India. “So we need to do more as South and South East Asian countries, and it’s something that needs better investigation, and it is leading to a misunderstanding of what the problem is.” 12:13pm - Expert says nutrition an issue of human capital, economic growth Dr Irshad Danish, the co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group, said that from his experience, Pakistan had low allocation, fragmented spending and implementation challenges. “If we need $10 to feed malnourished children, we are spending only $2,” he said. He added that Pakistan was losing $17bn annually due to malnutrition. He said that this also resulted in poor education outcomes, children with cognitive issues and lower workforce productivity. “So, nutrition is not just a health issue. It is an issue of human capital and economic growth,” he said. He said that the cost of malnutrition was far greater than the cost of prevention. “We need to move from fragmented spending towards strategic investment, and from hidden allocations to transparent budgets,” he said. Dr Irshad Danish. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 12:00pm - Doctor stresses importance of lady health workers Co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group Dr Irshad Danish stressed the significance of the lady health workers programme. “It was one of the strongest community based health workers model and its coverage was around 60pc, with over 100,000 lady health workers,” he said, adding that the workers enjoyed community ownership. “These workers were often the first link of access for healthcare [..] many independent evaluation where these health workers were available, there was better health knowledge and better access to essential services.” 11:46am - Sri Lankan official explains how country scaled health systems Dr Ravi Rannan-Eliya, the executive director of Sri Lanka’s Institute of Health Policy, said that 100 years ago, the South Asian country had worse health outcomes than the rest of the region. “We were the sick man of South Asia, but now we have the best health plan. How did that happen? One simple reason I always tell people was the ballot box ... the British decided to give self-rule,” he said. He said that as a consequence, there was a pressure to give free education and to expand health services. He said that voters prioritised access to care over all other things. Dr Ravi Rannan-Eliya. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzed 11:42am - Session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities The session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities has now begun. 11:30am- Scaling Up Nutrition movement official highlights its progress Asia Regional Representative of the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement Dr Srikanth Eadara spoke about the objectives of the movement, which he said was comprised of 67 countries and was a country-led global nutrition advocacy platform. “It unites different stakeholders coming from civil society, private sector, donors, UN, agencies and other entities as well as youth to end malnutrition,” he said, adding that it was launched in 2013 to “ ensure a coordinated multisectoral and multi-stakeholder action to address malnutrition in all its forms”. “We are currently in the fourth phase of the SUN Movement, and it is based on the current challenges and current context of nutrition, which shows that, yes, there is progress; however, the progress is slow and uneven,” he noted. Dr Eadara also spoke of the issues surrounding nutrition finance, highlighting that the cost of malnutrition was “estimated to be around 5 to 11pc of the total GDPs of Asia and Africa”. He warned that recent funding cuts, particularly in the World Health Organisation have “threatened to reverse progress” made on nutrition. “The reduction will also result in increased hardships and deaths, with a lot of implications for public health and economic growth and stability,” he said. 11:25am - Doctor says nutrition the ‘outcome of many systems’ Dr Aminah Jahangir, the global lead for health and nutrition at the Aga Khan Foundation, said that nutrition is the outcome of many systems and cannot be solved by one. She said that climate was already shaping the conditions in which children grow. “Our experience suggests that the outcomes are better where health services, food systems and community institutions have worked around the same household over many years. It reminds us that progress is achievable in our own context,” she said. 11:20am - Social protection can address malnutrition, says WFP official The WFP official spoke of one of the three priorities the organisation held for its work in South Asia was advocacy for policy engagement. She explained, “this is a continuous effort to work with governments from South Asia to highlight how social protection can be more than a safety net and more than a poverty reduction instrument”. Hobbs said that with the right intentions, social protection held promise to improve nutrition, diets and address malnutrition. “This is because social protection already reaches the families that are the most vulnerable and those are the families that face the highest challenges,” she added. Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 11:12am: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs, in her address, spoke of the geographical realities of stunting, stating that the majority of children affected by stunting are from middle-income countries. “Over 80pc of the world’s stunted children are in middle-income countries,” she said. The WFP official continued: “This means that low-income countries may have the highest rate and prevalence, but because middle-income countries have such a large population, it may have higher numbers of stunted children.” She stressed that the facts highlighted that stunting was a result of “inequalities within countries”. 11:05am - Expert highlights need for coordinated response Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, said that neither food nor the health systems could solve malnutrition alone. “Progress requires coordinated action across food systems, health systems and social protection. Countries that built integrated approaches before crisis struck, were able to keep essential services running through disruption,” he said. “Integration cannot be improvised during a crisis. It has to be done in advance,” he said. 11:00am - Expert says 2.6bn people cannot afford a healthy diet Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, presented a report on global nutrition. “Around the world, progress on nutrition is under increasing pressure. Climate shocks, conflict, economic uncertainty ... are affecting food and health systems,” he said. He said that the 2026 global nutrition report focused on how countries can build healthy diets, through stronger integration of food and health systems while building resilience. “Today, 2.6 billion cannot afford a healthy diet,” he said. He said that extreme weather, rising food prices and pressure on health services were arriving alongside conflict and instability, which was affecting food and health systems. 10:55am - Session on global and regional realities begins The session on global and regional realities has now begun. 10:52am - UN official says nutrition should not be activated only after a crisis Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that communities must be at the heart of the response to malnutrition and stunting. “Investing in front line workers and community-based platforms and listening to communities themselves can strengthen the uptake of essential services and practices, reinforce local ownership and ensure that women and children most at risk are reached,” she said. She said that Pakistan knew better than most how quickly climate disasters, economic shocks and displacement can undermine years of development programmes. “Nutrition, therefore, cannot be something we activate only after a crisis. It needs to be built into the preparedness, into the anticipatory action and the shock responsive systems so that vulnerable families are identified beforehand,” she said. ernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, addresses the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:46am - UN official says malnutrition an ‘emergency we can no longer ignore’ Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that malnutrition was an “emergency we can no longer ignore”. “When we talk about nutrition, we are not only talking about what a child eats. We are talking about whether a child reaches their full potential. We are talking about the strength of Pakistan’s capital. Nutrition is not only a health issue, it’s a development issue, an economic issue and an issue of equity and opportunity,” she said. She said that children living in poorer and remote areas were more likely to be left behind. She also said that at the same time, Pakistan faced a growing burden of obesity-related diseases. 10:40am - World Bank official says malnutrition barrier to health, prosperity of individuals, nations Abigail Perry, the lead nutrition specialist at the World Bank, said malnutrition was a fundamental barrier to the health and prosperity of individuals, communities and nations. “When a child’s development suffers early in life, the effects can last a lifetime,” she said. She said that the challenge for Pakistan was how to act at the scale, speed and quality required. 10:35am - WHO chief says nutrition is not just about food World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said nutrition was not only about food. “It is about access to safe, healthy, diets and strong food systems. Government, academia, civil society and the private sector all have a role to play,” he said. World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus’ video message plays during the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:30am - WHO chief says malnutrition one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a recorded message, said that malnutrition remained one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity. “Every year, it contributes to millions of preventable deaths,” he said. He said that the problem was not a lack of knowledge, rather a lack of action. 10:20am - Minister says equity begins in the womb Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that the Pakistan of 2047 is being built today. “It is being built in the health of our mothers. It is being built in the nutrition of our infants. It is being built in our homes and communities and it is being built in the developing minds and bodies of our youngest children,” he said. “We all have to work as a whole,” he said, calling for the conference to spur action. “Let this be our commitment: every child nourished is protected, every child given a fair start brings Pakistan one step closer to the future we seek,” he said. 10:10am - Minister says investment in nutrition is not charity “Pakistan cannot win the economic race of the 21st century if millions of children begin the race of life several steps behind than others. There can be no knowledge economy without developing the capacity of the human brain. There can be no productivity revolution without healthy and capable workers. There can be no genuine equality if inequality begins before a child is even born,” said Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal. “Therefore, investment in nutrition is not charity, it is economic policy,” he said. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal addresses the conference as the guest speaker. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:03am - Minister says first 5 years of a child’s life critical Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that human resource development had not been prioritised in the past. He appreciated the initiative by DawnMedia Group to address the nutrition crisis and called on civil society to take up social issues. “90 per cent of a children’s brain develops by the age of five .. so the first five years in the life of a child are the most critical,” he said. “If we fail to develop that human infrastructure during the earliest years of life, we weaken every other investment we subsequently make,” he said. “That is why stunting cannot remain merely a statistic. For the planning minister, it is a national development challenge,” he said. 9:57am - Planning minister says quality of human resource critical for countries In his remarks, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, the chief guest, conveyed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s firm commitment to addressing malnutrition and stunting as a national development priority. He said that as the planning minister, he spent much of his time dealing with the architecture of Pakistan’s development. “We discuss motorways, energy, dams and digital networks. All of these are essential, but there is one investment more fundamental than all others: the investment in human development,” he said. “Ultimately it is humans and people who build nations. articles.title: Syria: Why continuity of care matters at Al-Bab Primary Health Care Centre
articles.description: Country: Syrian Arab Republic Source: World Health Organization 31 August 2026, Aleppo, Syrian Arab Republic: When Abdul Hamid Taleb comes to Al-Bab Primary Health Care Centre, he is not looking for a cure. He is living with type 2 diabetes. What he needs is something quieter, but no less important: somewhere he can return to regularly to check his blood sugar, review his health and make sure a condition he lives with every day remains under control. In May 2026, Abdul Hamid visited the internal medicine clinic for one of these follow-up consultations. “Diabetes is something I know I have to keep watching,” he says. “I cannot wait until I feel very unwell before I think about it. I need to know that my sugar is controlled and that I am doing what I should.” Following a clinical assessment, the health team reviewed his treatment and prescribed medicines to help regulate his blood sugar and reduce the risk of vascular complications. They also spoke with him about the parts of diabetes management that happen outside the consultation room: taking his medicines consistently, reducing sugar and refined carbohydrates in his diet, staying physically active and continuing to monitor his blood glucose. For Abdul Hamid, these regular conversations are part of living with a chronic illness. “When you come for follow-up, you understand your condition better,” he says. “They tell me what I need to continue doing and what I need to pay attention to. That helps me feel that I am managing my health, rather than waiting for something to go wrong.” For people living with diabetes and other noncommunicable diseases, this continuity can be critical. Missed monitoring or interruptions in treatment can allow a manageable condition to progress, increasing the risk of complications and, eventually, the need for more specialized care. Across the same clinic, however, not everyone comes with a diagnosis they already know. Knowing when something needs attention Mohammad Hallaq came to the internal medicine clinic in June this year after experiencing general fatigue and discomfort. Following an examination, health workers found signs consistent with varicose veins, a condition that can cause heaviness, aching and fatigue in the legs. Mohammad received treatment for pain when needed, but much of the consultation focused on things he could do himself: elevating his legs while resting, avoiding standing for long periods, incorporating light walking into his routine and returning to the clinic for follow-up. “I came because I was tired and wanted to understand why,” Mohammad says. “Sometimes you keep going and assume the discomfort will pass. It was useful to have someone examine me and explain what I could do.” The advice was straightforward, but that was part of its value. “Not everything needs complicated treatment,” he adds. “Sometimes knowing how to manage the problem, and knowing when you need to come back, is what you need.” A few weeks later, Amina Khazma arrived at the same clinic with another common but unsettling combination of symptoms: fatigue and headache. After examining her, the medical team assessed her headache as tension-related. She was given treatment to relieve the pain and advised to rest, drink sufficient fluids and reduce sources of stress and physical strain where possible. Importantly, she was also told to return if the headache persisted or became more severe. “When you have a headache and you are tired, you do not always know whether it is something simple or something you should worry about,” Amina says. “Being examined gave me reassurance.” For her, knowing what to watch for was as important as receiving medicine. “They explained what I could do at home and when I should come back,” she says. “It means you do not have to sit with the worry on your own.” Care before crisis For Dr Jamal Alwan, who sees patients at Al-Bab Primary Health Care Centre, these different consultations are part of what primary health care is meant to do. “People do not all arrive with the same needs,” he says. “One person may be living with diabetes and need regular follow-up. Another may have pain or fatigue and not know what is causing it. Our role is to assess them, provide the care they need and help them understand what they can do to protect their health.” That can mean treatment. It can also mean monitoring, reassurance, health advice or recognizing when someone needs further investigation or referral. “The earlier people come, the more options we often have,” Dr Alwan says. “Primary health care is not only about treating illness after it becomes severe. It is also about following chronic diseases, recognizing problems early and helping people manage their health before complications develop.” In communities where years of crisis have damaged health infrastructure and strained household finances, having that first point of care available cannot be taken for granted. Al-Bab Primary Health Care Centre is one of 70 centres across Aleppo, Idleb, Hama and Homs supported through a WHO project funded by KSrelief. The project helps keep services running by supporting health workers and operational costs, alongside medicines, medical supplies and specialized care. Across the project, around 800 medical and non-medical personnel are supported, including more than 450 physicians, nurses and other health professionals. Since November 2025, KSrelief’s support has enabled around 475,000 consultations, 260,000 medicine-related services, 51,000 laboratory tests and 35,000 dialysis sessions, helping sustain primary health care and life-saving dialysis services. Forty-four supported facilities are also applying protocols for noncommunicable diseases, strengthening the regular, long-term care people like Abdul Hamid rely on. Keeping these services available also supports Syria’s broader health system transition. WHO is working with the Ministry of Health and partners to strengthen primary health care, improve integration and quality, and move towards a more nationally owned health system, while helping ensure that immediate gaps in staffing, medicines and essential services do not disrupt care today. For Dr Alwan, those ambitions become tangible one consultation at a time. “It is the person sitting in front of you who matters at that moment,” he says. “Maybe they need continued treatment. Maybe they need an examination and reassurance. Maybe they simply need someone to explain what is happening and what they should do next. What matters is that the service is here when they need it.” At Al-Bab Primary Health Care Centre, that continuity is what turns routine consultations into something more lasting: the chance to manage illness early, protect health and avoid preventable complications.

articles.description: A two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’, is being held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel on Pakistan’s persistent nutrition and stunting crisis. With more than 40 per cent of children under five stunted, a maternal mortality rate of 155 deaths per 100,000 live births, and malnutrition costing Pakistan upwards of $17 billion annually, the country stands at a crossroads: continue on the current trajectory and surrender an entire generation’s potential, or choose a different future. The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action. The focus of discussions will be on moving the national conversation beyond statistics towards practical, measurable interventions that can improve nutrition outcomes and protect Pakis­tan’s human capital and future generations. View the full agenda here . 11:46am - Sri Lankan official explains how country scaled health systems Ravi Rannan-Eliya, the executive director of Sri Lanka’s Institute of Health Policy, said that 100 years ago, the South Asian country had worse health outcomes than the rest of the region. “We were the sick man of South Asia, but now we have the best health plan. How did that happen? One simple reason I always tell people was the ballot box ... the British decided to give self-rule,” he said. He said that as a consequence, there was a pressure to give free education and to expand health services. He said that voters prioritised access to care over all other things. 11:42am - Session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities The session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities has now begun. 11:30am- Scaling Up Nutrition movement official highlights its progress Asia Regional Representative of the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement Dr Srikanth Eadara spoke about the objectives of the movement, which he said was comprised of 67 countries and was a country-led global nutrition advocacy platform. “It unites different stakeholders coming from civil society, private sector, donors, UN, agencies and other entities as well as youth to end malnutrition,” he said, adding that it was launched in 2013 to “ ensure a coordinated multisectoral and multi-stakeholder action to address malnutrition in all its forms”. “We are currently in the fourth phase of the SUN Movement, and it is based on the current challenges and current context of nutrition, which shows that, yes, there is progress; however, the progress is slow and uneven,” he noted. Dr Eadara also spoke of the issues surrounding nutrition finance, highlighting that the cost of malnutrition was “estimated to be around 5 to 11pc of the total GDPs of Asia and Africa”. He warned that recent funding cuts, particularly in the World Health Organisation have “threatened to reverse progress” made on nutrition. “The reduction will also result in increased hardships and deaths, with a lot of implications for public health and economic growth and stability,” he said. 11:25am - Doctor says nutrition the ‘outcome of many systems’ Dr Aminah Jahangir, the global lead for health and nutrition at the Aga Khan Foundation, said that nutrition is the outcome of many systems and cannot be solved by one. She said that climate was already shaping the conditions in which children grow. “Our experience suggests that the outcomes are better where health services, food systems and community institutions have worked around the same household over many years. It reminds us that progress is achievable in our own context,” she said. 11:20am - Social protection can address malnutrition, says WFP official The WFP official spoke of one of the three priorities the organisation held for its work in South Asia in South Asia were advocacy for policy engagement. She explained, “this is a continuous effort to work with governments from South Asia to highlight how social protection can be more than a safety net and more than a poverty reduction instrument”. Hobbs said that with the right intentions, social protection held promise to improve nutrition, diets and address malnutrition. “This is because social protection already reaches the families that are the most vulnerable and those are the families that face the highest challenges,” she added. The WFP official continued: “This means that low-income countries may have the highest rate and prevalence, but because middle-income countries have such a large population, it may have higher numbers of stunted children.” She stressed that the facts highlighted that stunting was a result of “inequalities within countries”. 11:05am - Expert highlights need for coordinated response Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, said that neither food nor the health systems could solve malnutrition alone. “Progress requires coordinated action across food systems, health systems and social protection. Countries that built integrated approaches before crisis struck, were able to keep essential services running through disruption,” he said. “Integration cannot be improvised during a crisis. It has to be done in advance,” he said. 11:00am - Expert says 2.6bn people cannot afford a healthy diet Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, presented a report on global nutrition. “Around the world, progress on nutrition is under increasing pressure. Climate shocks, conflict, economic uncertainty ... are affecting food and health systems,” he said. He said that the 2026 global nutrition report focused on how countries can build healthy diets, through stronger integration of food and health systems while building resilience. “Today, 2.6 billion cannot afford a healthy diet,” he said. He said that extreme weather, rising food prices and pressure on health services were arriving alongside conflict and instability, which was affecting food and health systems. 10:55am - Session on global and regional realities begins The session on global and regional realities has now begun. 10:52am - UN official says nutrition should not be activated only after a crisis Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that communities must be at the heart of the response to malnutrition and stunting. “Investing in front line workers and community-based platforms and listening to communities themselves can strengthen the uptake of essential services and practices, reinforce local ownership and ensure that women and children most at risk are reached,” she said. She said that Pakistan knew better than most how quickly climate disasters, economic shocks and displacement can undermine years of development programmes. “Nutrition, therefore, cannot be something we activate only after a crisis. It needs to be built into the preparedness, into the anticipatory action and the shock responsive systems so that vulnerable families are identified beforehand,” she said. ernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, addresses the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:46am - UN official says malnutrition an ‘emergency we can no longer ignore’ Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that malnutrition was an “emergency we can no longer ignore”. “When we talk about nutrition, we are not only talking about what a child eats. She said that children living in poorer and remote areas were more likely to be left behind. She also said that at the same time, Pakistan faced a growing burden of obesity-related diseases. 10:40am - World Bank official says malnutrition barrier to health, prosperity of individuals, nations Abigail Perry, the lead nutrition specialist at the World Bank, said malnutrition was a fundamental barrier to the health and prosperity of individuals, communities and nations. “When a child’s development suffers early in life, the effects can last a lifetime,” she said. She said that the challenge for Pakistan was how to act at the scale, speed and quality required. 10:35am - WHO chief says nutrition is not just about food World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said nutrition was not only about food. “It is about access to safe, healthy, diets and strong food systems. Government, academia, civil society and the private sector all have a role to play,” he said. World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus’ video message plays during the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:30am - WHO chief says malnutrition one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a recorded message, said that malnutrition remained one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity. “Every year, it contributes to millions of preventable deaths,” he said. He said that the problem was not a lack of knowledge, rather a lack of action. 10:20am - Minister says equity begins in the womb Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that the Pakistan of 2047 is being built today. “It is being built in the health of our mothers. It is being built in the nutrition of our infants. It is being built in our homes and communities and it is being built in the developing minds and bodies of our youngest children,” he said. “We all have to work as a whole,” he said, calling for the conference to spur action. “Let this be our commitment: every child nourished is protected, every child given a fair start brings Pakistan one step closer to the future we seek,” he said. 10:10am - Minister says investment in nutrition is not charity “Pakistan cannot win the economic race of the 21st century if millions of children begin the race of life several steps behind than others. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal addresses the conference as the guest speaker. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:03am - Minister says first 5 years of a child’s life critical Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that human resource development had not been prioritised in the past. articles.title: Free cholesterol tests on the NHS are great – but here’s the five-point health MOT I’d really like to see | Devi Sridhar
articles.description: You could be walking around symptom-free and not know you’re pre-diabetic, living with hypertension or at a high risk of a heart attack Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh “An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure,” Benjamin Franklin’s adage goes. Yet that simple prescription has been hard to follow in the current NHS. As has been frequently highlighted , one of the biggest challenges for the health system is not just how much we spend per capita, but where and when it is spent. In England, there has been an ongoing shift within the NHS budget towards acute hospital care – treating people in hospitals, often after they are already quite ill – while funding for primary care such as GPs has fallen. The consequence is that the NHS is increasingly paying for serious and expensive disease treatment, rather than investing upstream to prevent disease in the first place. We spend heavily on dealing with heart attacks, strokes and other life-threatening conditions, rather than identifying those who are at higher risk and intervening earlier to reduce their chances of getting ill. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...
